title: A first look at your data
text:
On this page, you copy data to Crunchomics, count the reads in every sample, make a quality report, and decide whether something looks off.
You do this first with the practice data from The commands you need. Then, if you already have your own sequencing data, you can repeat the same steps with your own data, as explained in Now your own data.
Two kinds of boxes on this page are closed. Open them only when you need them:
Keep notes as you go. Copy each command you run into a text file, with a few words about what you saw. The CLI workshop explains how. If something looks off and you ask someone for help later, these notes help a lot.

section: Step 1: Log in and make a practice folder
text:
Step 1: Log in and make a practice folder
Crunchomics is the High Performance Computer (HPC) of the UvA: a group of powerful computers that you use through the terminal. Your sequencing files are large, and the tools you need are already installed there. With ssh, you connect your terminal to Crunchomics. After that, every command you type runs on Crunchomics, not on your own computer, until you log out.

# On your computer: log in to Crunchomics (on eduroam or with the VPN)
# Replace uvanetid with your own UvAnetID
# You won't see anything happening when you type your password, that is normal
ssh uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl

If ssh asks whether you want to continue connecting, type yes and press Enter. After you log in, the prompt changes: it now shows your UvAnetID and omics-h0. This is how you know that your commands run on Crunchomics. To log out, type exit. More: ssh in the CLI workshop.
If this is your first time on Crunchomics, set up your account once. A script adds the installed software to your PATH (the list of folders where bash looks for programs) and makes the personal folder that you use below. Skip this if you did it before, for example in the CLI workshop.

# On Crunchomics: run the setup script (only once per account)
/zfs/omics/software/script/omics_install_script

# Check: you should now see a line that ends with personal -> /zfs/omics/personal/uvanetid
ls -lh

More: preparing your account in the CLI workshop.
Now make a practice folder in your personal folder, with a data folder for the sequencing files and a results folder for everything you make:

# On Crunchomics: go to your personal folder
# It has 500 GB of space, your home folder only 25 GB, so keep your data here
cd ~/personal

# Make the practice folder with a data and a results folder inside
# The -p also makes seq_qc_practice if it does not exist yet, and gives no error if it already exists
mkdir -p seq_qc_practice/data seq_qc_practice/results

# Move into the practice folder
cd seq_qc_practice

# Check: you should be in /home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc_practice (with your UvAnetID), and see data and results
pwd
ls







Fixcd: personal: No such file or directory





Your account is not set up yet, so the personal folder does not exist. Run the setup script above, then try cd ~/personal again.



From now on, run every command on Crunchomics from inside the seq_qc_practice folder. If you log out and in again, first go back with cd ~/personal/seq_qc_practice.

section: Step 2: Copy the practice data to Crunchomics
text:
Step 2: Copy the practice data to Crunchomics
You copy practice_data.tar.gz from your own computer to Crunchomics with scp. This is the same command you can use later for your own data.
You must run scp in a terminal on your own computer, because that is where the file is. So open a second terminal on your own computer, and keep the first one logged in to Crunchomics:

MobaXterm (Windows): click the + next to your open tab. A new tab opens on your own computer.
WSL (Windows): click the + at the top of the Ubuntu window. If the new tab opens PowerShell instead of Ubuntu, click the small arrow next to the + and choose Ubuntu.
Mac: in Terminal, press Command-N.




Two terminals in MobaXterm: one tab on your own computer, one tab logged in to Crunchomics (omics-h0), and the + to open a new tab.


In the second terminal:

# On your computer: go to the practice folder in your home folder
cd ~/seq_qc_practice

# Copy the practice data into the practice folder on Crunchomics
# Replace both instances of uvanetid with your UvAnetID
scp practice_data.tar.gz uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc_practice/

An scp command has two parts: first what you copy (the source), then where it goes (the destination). Here, the source is practice_data.tar.gz in the folder you are in. The destination is your practice folder on Crunchomics. Before the : is your login, as with ssh, and after the : is the path on Crunchomics. scp asks for your password again, and again you do not see anything while you type. More: scp in the CLI workshop.






TipTip: Download the practice data directly onto Crunchomics (optional)





If you did not download the practice data on your own computer, download it directly onto Crunchomics instead:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice: download the practice data
curl -L -O "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/sequencing_qc/main/data/practice_data.tar.gz"




Now go back to the terminal that is logged in to Crunchomics, and unpack the file:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
# Check: is practice_data.tar.gz there, and how large is it?
ls -lh

# Unpack it: -x extract, -z it is compressed (.gz), -f the file name follows
tar -xzf practice_data.tar.gz

# Check: which files and folders do you see now?
ls -lh







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result






Before unpacking: practice_data.tar.gz, with a size of about 11M (11 megabytes), and the empty data and results folders.
After unpacking: data, results, practice_data.tar.gz and seqkit_stats_practice.tsv.




The practice data has two parts:

A small set of fastq files in data, in one folder per sample (32 samples, each reduced to 2% of its reads). You use them to try the tools in Steps 3 and 5.
seqkit_stats_practice.tsv: the full read-count table of the original runs (364 samples). You use it for the read-count check in Step 4.


Move the files out of the sample folders
All commands on this page expect the fastq.gz files directly in data, for example data/*.fastq.gz. As on your own computer, move the fastq.gz files directly into data and remove the empty sample folders. See Tidy up: mv and rmdir if you need a reminder.

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
# Count the fastq.gz files in the sample folders
ls data/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

# Move them up into the data folder. -n: never overwrite a file that already exists
mv -n data/*/*.fastq.gz data/

# Count the fastq.gz files directly in data: the same number as before
ls data/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

# Remove the empty sample folders. rmdir only removes empty folders
rmdir data/*/

# Check: data should now contain only fastq.gz files
ls data | head
ls data | wc -l







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result






64 fastq.gz files in the sample folders, and 64 directly in data after mv.
After rmdir, ls data | wc -l also gives 64: no folders are left.






Check: are all files there?
The fastq.gz files should sit directly in the data folder. With paired-end sequencing, each sample has one R1 and one R2 file.

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
# Look at the first file names
ls data | head

# Count all fastq.gz files
ls data/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

# Count the R1 and the R2 files: these numbers should be the same
# The second * also finds names with more text after R1, for example Sample1_R1_001.fastq.gz
ls data/*_R1*.fastq.gz | wc -l
ls data/*_R2*.fastq.gz | wc -l







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





64 fastq.gz files: 32 R1 files and 32 R2 files. So the practice data has 32 samples.

title: A first look at your data
text:
Step 3: Count reads with seqkit
seqkit stats makes one table with the number of reads and their quality for every file. It is installed on Crunchomics. The CLI workshop explains the options in detail.
Before you run this software, you need to know how Crunchomics works, because it has two kinds of computers. When you log in, you are on the login node. Everyone shares it, so use it only for small tasks, like moving around and looking at files. As a rule of thumb, a task that needs only one CPU and finishes in less than an hour can run on the login node. Heavier work, like counting all reads, runs on a compute node. The command srun sends your command to such a compute node. The options after srun say how much the command may use: the number of CPUs (processors that work at the same time), the memory, and the maximum time. The tools you run here are not very heavy and you can typically use the exact same settings for your own data.
More: login node and compute nodes and srun in the CLI workshop.






ImportantImportant: keep the terminal open until the prompt comes back





srun waits until the command is done. If you close the terminal, lose the connection, or your laptop goes to sleep, the command stops halfway. With the practice data, this takes a few minutes. Keep the terminal open and your laptop awake until you see the prompt again.




# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
mkdir -p results/seqkit

# Run seqkit stats on a compute node, with 4 CPUs
# -j 4: seqkit uses the 4 CPUs that srun asks for
# The \ at the end of the first line means: the command continues on the next line.
# Copy both lines together.
# While the command runs, you see nothing. Wait until the prompt comes back.
srun --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G --time=01:00:00 \
    seqkit stats -b -a -T -j 4 -o results/seqkit/seqkit_stats.tsv data/*.fastq.gz

# Check: one header line plus one line per fastq.gz file
wc -l results/seqkit/seqkit_stats.tsv

# Look at the table. Use the arrow keys to scroll, and q to quit
column -t results/seqkit/seqkit_stats.tsv | less -S

If you type the srun command yourself, put nothing after the \, not even a space.
The most important column for now is num_seqs, the number of reads in each file. Scroll through it. Do you see files with far fewer reads than the others?






AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





65 lines: one header line and 64 files.
Most Run1_ samples up to Run1_S152 have about 1,000 to 2,700 reads. From Run1_S153 on, the samples have between 0 and 18 reads, and Run1_S154 has none at all. The three Run2_ samples have about 550 reads each.



These numbers are small because every file was reduced to 2% of its reads. With these reduced files, almost every sample would fall below the 1,000-read flag in Step 4. That is why you use the full practice table in Step 4.

title: A first look at your data
text:
Step 4: The read-count check
This is the most important step. You look for samples with far fewer reads than the rest.
In this step, you use the full practice table, seqkit_stats_practice.tsv, with all 364 samples of the original runs.

4a: R1 and R2 have the same number of reads
For paired-end data, every read in the R1 file has a partner in the R2 file. So both files of a sample must have the same number of reads.

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
# Make two files that store the read numbers of all R1 files, and of all R2 files, in the same order
grep "_R1" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | cut -f4 > results/seqkit/r1_counts.txt
grep "_R2" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | cut -f4 > results/seqkit/r2_counts.txt

# Put them side by side and count the lines where they differ. Expected: 0
paste results/seqkit/r1_counts.txt results/seqkit/r2_counts.txt | awk '$1 != $2' | wc -l







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





0: R1 and R2 have the same number of reads in every sample.









FixIf the result is not 0: what to check





First check in Step 2 that the numbers of R1 and R2 files are the same. The command above compares the files line by line. If one R1 or R2 file is missing, every line after it is shifted, and many lines differ.
Some files may also be incomplete. This often happens when a download or a copy breaks off halfway. Test whether the files are complete:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
# This uses one CPU, so it can run on the login node, without srun
# Test every fastq.gz file. gzip -t prints nothing if a file is complete,
# and an error message (for example "unexpected end of file") if it is not 
# If all is good then you only see the name of the fastq.gz files on the screen
for f in data/*.fastq.gz; do
    echo "$f"
    gzip -t "$f"
done

Download or copy the broken files again, and run Steps 3 and 4 again. If the new files are still broken, contact the sequencing center. Also contact the sequencing center if all files are complete and the read numbers of R1 and R2 still differ.





4b: Reads per sample, from low to high
Next, you make a new file that only stores the number of reads per file, to make some comparisons. For this, you only use the R1 files, so that each sample is counted once.

# Take the file name (column 1) and the number of reads (column 4) of all R1 files,
# and sort from the lowest to the highest number of reads
cut -f1,4 seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | grep "_R1" | sort -t$'\t' -k2,2n > results/read_counts.tsv

# Check: one line per sample
wc -l results/read_counts.tsv

# The 10 samples with the fewest reads, and the 5 with the most
head results/read_counts.tsv
tail -5 results/read_counts.tsv







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





364 lines, one per sample. The samples with the fewest reads have only 10 to 40 reads. The samples with the most reads have more than 150,000.





4c: Which samples have very few reads?
A sample is flagged if it has fewer than 1,000 reads, or fewer than 10% of the median number of reads. You check the two flags one after the other.
First, you store the name of the file to check in a variable. A variable stores a piece of text under a short name. $counts then stands for that text. If you later want to check another file, for example one sequencing run on its own (see 4f), you only change this one line. More: variables in the CLI workshop.
Variables are lost when you log out or close the terminal. If you continue later, first run the commands of 4c again. Without them, the commands below give wrong results without an error: they print 0 or nothing, or they seem to hang. If a command seems to hang, press Ctrl+C to stop it.
Start with the first flag:

# The read-count file to check: all samples, sorted from low to high
counts=results/read_counts.tsv

# Flag 1: how many samples have fewer than 1000 reads?
# -F'\t': the columns are separated by tabs. '$2 < 1000': keep lines where column 2 is below 1000
awk -F'\t' '$2 < 1000' "$counts" | wc -l







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





104 samples have fewer than 1,000 reads.



A fixed number does not fit every dataset. If the median is 200,000 reads, a sample with 5,000 reads has clearly failed, but it still has more than 1,000 reads. So you also compare each sample with the median. The median is the read number of the sample in the middle of the sorted list. Unlike the average, it is not pulled down by a few failed samples.

# The median: the read number on the middle line of the sorted file
n_samples=$(wc -l < "$counts")
middle=$(( (n_samples + 1) / 2 ))
median=$(sed -n "${middle}p" "$counts" | cut -f2)

# The limit: 10% of the median
limit=$(( median / 10 ))
echo "samples: $n_samples  median: $median  10% of median: $limit"

# Flag 2: how many samples have fewer reads than 10% of the median?
awk -F'\t' -v limit="$limit" '$2 < limit' "$counts" | wc -l







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





364 samples, a median of 30,149 reads and a limit of 3,014. 108 samples fall below the limit: the 104 samples from flag 1, plus 4 samples with between 1,000 and 3,014 reads.





4d: Do the flagged samples form a pattern?
A few scattered samples with low reads are normal: some samples simply contain little DNA. You do not need to contact anyone about them. Still, write them down. Later, in your analysis, you decide what to do with them, for example remove them, or keep them and check whether they change your results. A block of samples with consecutive numbers is a warning sign. It points to a problem with a group of samples that were handled together, for example one part of a plate.

# The flagged samples, sorted by name instead of by reads
# sort -V sorts numbers in names the way people do (S9 before S10)
awk -F'\t' -v limit="$limit" '$2 < limit' "$counts" | sort -V | column -t







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





In run 1, the flagged samples form clear blocks: Run1_S057 to Run1_S095, Run1_S153 to Run1_S191 and Run1_S249 to Run1_S280. The samples were on three 96-well plates, and on every plate, columns 8 to 12 failed. This is a clear reason to go through the checklist in Step 6.
In run 2, 6 samples are flagged. Three are blanks, which is expected (see 4e). The other three (Run2_ITS097, Run2_ITS175, Run2_ITS178) are scattered, with about 1,000 to 2,500 reads. That is worth a note for your analysis, but not alarming.





4e: Blanks and controls
Blanks (negative controls) should have clearly fewer reads than your samples. The command looks for common names for controls:

# Lines with blank, neg, ntc, control or mock in the name (upper or lower case)
grep -i -E "blank|neg|ntc|control|mock" "$counts"

A blank with as many reads as a normal sample can mean contamination. A positive control (for example a mock community) with very few reads can mean that the PCR did not work well.






AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





5 lines, all from run 2. Run 1 of the practice data has no controls.

Three blanks have few reads (41, 126 and 237), as expected.
One blank, Run2_ITS191_PCR_Blank, has 4,561 reads, which is high for a blank. Worth mentioning.
Run2_ITS192_PCR_Control has 30,798 reads, close to the median. If this is a positive control, that is a good sign.






4f: More than one sequencing run? (optional)
Sequencing runs can differ a lot in how many reads they give. If your data comes from more than one run, the median of all samples together may not fit each run.






TipTip: Check each sequencing run on its own (optional)





The practice table contains two runs. The file names start with the run (Run1_ or Run2_), so you can split the table by name. For your own data, see Now your own data to find out which run each file comes from.

# One read-count file per run
# The ^ means "at the start of the line"
grep "^Run1_" results/read_counts.tsv > results/read_counts_run1.tsv
grep "^Run2_" results/read_counts.tsv > results/read_counts_run2.tsv

# Check: the number of samples per run
wc -l results/read_counts_run1.tsv results/read_counts_run2.tsv

Then set counts to one run, and run the commands of 4c, 4d and 4e again. Repeat for the other run:

# Check run 1 on its own
counts=results/read_counts_run1.tsv

# After 4c to 4e for run 1: check run 2 on its own
counts=results/read_counts_run2.tsv







AnswerPractice data: compare with your result






Run 1: 240 samples, a median of 95,605 reads and a limit of 9,560. 102 samples fall below the limit.
Run 2: 124 samples, a median of 29,236 reads and a limit of 2,923. 6 samples fall below the limit.

The two medians differ by a factor of three. Still, the flagged samples are the same 108 as in 4c, because the failed samples have far fewer reads than any of the limits. With other data, a run can have samples that pass the limit of all samples together, but fall below the limit of their own run. This is most likely when one run gives many more reads than the other.

title: A first look at your data
text:
Step 5: Quality reports with FastQC
FastQC makes a quality report for every fastq file. You open a few of these reports in your browser (5b) and look for samples that stand out (5c). If you have many samples, you can also combine all reports into one with MultiQC (5d, optional).

5a: FastQC
FastQC is installed on Crunchomics. As in Step 3, keep the terminal open until the prompt comes back.

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice
mkdir -p results/fastqc

# Run FastQC on all fastq.gz files, on a compute node with 8 CPUs
# --threads 8: FastQC uses the 8 CPUs that srun asks for. Copy both lines together.
srun --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=16G --time=02:00:00 \
    fastqc data/*.fastq.gz -o results/fastqc --threads 8

# Check: one html report per fastq.gz file, so these two numbers should be the same
ls results/fastqc/*.html | wc -l
ls data/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

As a rough guide, about 700 files from a MiSeq amplicon run took about 20 minutes with 10 CPUs. Small runs, like the practice data, finish in a few minutes.






AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





64 html reports and 64 fastq.gz files.





5b: Open a few reports
With many samples, you do not need to look at every report. Pick a few that tell you the most:

Two or three typical samples, with a read number close to the median
The samples with the fewest reads, especially if they were flagged in Step 4
Your blanks and controls

For the practice data, compare a good sample, Run1_S137_R1_fastqc.html, with a failed one, Run1_S158_R1_fastqc.html (10 reads), and with the empty Run1_S154_R1_fastqc.html. The FastQC report of a file has the same name as the file, but ends in _fastqc.html instead of .fastq.gz.
Open a typical sample first, so that you know what “normal” looks like for your data. Then compare the others with it. Choose one of the two ways to open the reports:

RStudio in your browserCopy with scp


Crunchomics also runs RStudio, a program that you use in your web browser. Its file browser lets you open the reports with a few clicks, without any commands.

In your web browser, go to omics-app01.science.uva.nl (on eduroam or with the VPN, as for ssh).
Sign in with your UvAnetID and your UvA password, the same as for ssh.
In the Files pane at the bottom right, click personal, then seq_qc_practice, then results, then fastqc.
Click the name of a report that ends in _fastqc.html, and choose View in Web Browser. The report opens in a new browser tab.




RStudio on Crunchomics. The Files pane (bottom right) shows the fastqc folder. A click on a report opens a menu with View in Web Browser.


RStudio signs you out after 60 minutes without activity. Then just sign in again.


Copy the reports to your own computer, as in Step 2. Run this in a terminal on your own computer, once per report:

# On your computer: go to the practice folder in your home folder
cd ~/seq_qc_practice

# Copy one FastQC report into the current folder. The . at the end means "the current folder"
# Replace both instances of uvanetid with your UvAnetID, and the file name with the report you want
scp uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc_practice/results/fastqc/Run1_S137_R1_fastqc.html .

# Check: the report is there
ls -lh *.html

To open the report, open the current folder in the file browser of your computer. Then double-click the html file, and it opens in your web browser:

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Windows (MobaXterm or WSL): open the current folder in File Explorer
explorer.exe .

# Mac: open the current folder in Finder
open .

Use the command for your own system. More: the file browser in the CLI workshop.





5c: What to look at in the reports
FastQC and MultiQC mark many things in yellow or red. For amplicon data, much of that is normal. Focus on whether some samples look clearly different from the rest.
Usually normal for amplicon data (no need to worry):

Per base sequence content fails: all reads start with the same primer, so the first bases are the same in every read
Sequence duplication is high, and overrepresented sequences are listed: amplicons are many copies of a few sequences. The overrepresented sequences often start with your primer
Per sequence GC content does not look like a smooth bell curve: the GC content depends on which organisms are in the sample
Quality goes down towards the end of the reads, more in R2 than in R1. Long reads (for example 2x300 bp on a MiSeq) often end in the yellow or red zone
Some adapter content at the end of the reads, if your amplicon is shorter than the read length

If you want to know what a panel shows, the FastQC help has one page per panel. It is written for all kinds of sequencing data, so a warning there does not always mean a problem for amplicon data (see the list above). The deeper dive shows a few panels of the practice data.
Worth a closer look:

Sequence counts: samples with far fewer reads than the rest (you already checked this in Step 4)
A group of samples with clearly lower quality than all others
Reports with Total Sequences 0: the file is empty. FastQC still makes a report, but the plots are empty and values like “File type: null” mean nothing
Quality that is low already at the start of the reads, in many samples

Samples with very few reads often also look worse in the quality plots. That is usually a side effect of having few reads, not a separate problem. The read-count check from Step 4 is the more reliable signal.


5d: One report for all samples with MultiQC (optional)
MultiQC combines all FastQC reports into one report. This makes it easier to compare many samples at once. It needs a bit more setup: MultiQC is not installed on Crunchomics for everyone, so you install it yourself with conda. Conda is a program that installs software into separate environments: folders with one tool and everything it needs, so that tools do not get in each other’s way. You only do this once. Afterwards, you can use MultiQC for every new sequencing run.






TipTip: Install MultiQC (only needed once)






Install conda. Follow the steps in Install Miniforge in the CLI workshop. If you already use conda on Crunchomics, skip this step.
Make an environment with MultiQC:


# On Crunchomics: make an environment called multiqc_1.35 and install MultiQC version 1.35 into it
# Press Y and Enter when mamba asks you to confirm
mamba create -n multiqc_1.35 -c conda-forge -c bioconda multiqc=1.35


Check that it works:


# Activate the environment, print the MultiQC version, and leave the environment again
conda activate multiqc_1.35
multiqc --version
conda deactivate

This should print the version, 1.35. More about environments: mamba create in the CLI workshop.



Now make the report:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc_practice: make one report from all FastQC reports
# MultiQC uses one CPU and finishes quickly, so it can run on the login node, without srun
mkdir -p results/multiqc
conda activate multiqc_1.35
multiqc results/fastqc -o results/multiqc
conda deactivate

# Check: the folder should contain multiqc_report.html
ls -lh results/multiqc

Open multiqc_report.html as in 5b: in RStudio, go to results, then multiqc. Or copy it with scp, in a terminal on your own computer:

# On your computer: go to the practice folder, and copy the MultiQC report into it
# Replace both instances of uvanetid with your UvAnetID
cd ~/seq_qc_practice
scp uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc_practice/results/multiqc/multiqc_report.html .

title: A first look at your data
text:
Step 6: Decide
Also read the delivery report. Many sequencing centers send a report with the read number per sample, and sometimes a warning about low samples. You do not need the command line for that, and it is easy to miss in a long email.
If nothing stands out: good news. Write down the date and the main numbers (number of samples, median reads, number of flagged samples) in your notes, and continue with your analysis.
If something stands out, act now. Most problems can still be explained or fixed in the first weeks: the leftover DNA and libraries still exist, and people still remember what they did. Open the box below that matches your problem. Each box says what to check and who to contact.
For the practice data, run 1 clearly has “many samples with few reads, in a block”. With your own data, this is where you would start to check your lab records.






FixFiles are missing, or the number of R1 and R2 files differs (Step 2)






Compare the file names with your sample sheet. Are the missing samples ones that you sent?
Download or copy the data again. Downloads can break off without a clear error.
Some sequencing centers send checksums with the data, often in a file ending in .md5. A checksum is a short code that is calculated from a file. If the code of your copy matches the code from the center, your copy is complete. Ask Nina if you are unsure how to compare them.

Who to contact: the sequencing center.









FixR1 and R2 of a sample have different read numbers (4a)






Test the files and download them again, as explained in the box in 4a.

Who to contact: the sequencing center, if the new files are still broken.









FixMany samples have few reads, or they form a block (4c and 4d)





Go through your lab records, step by step. For each step, compare the flagged samples with the other samples:

DNA extraction: the DNA concentrations. Were they already low for the flagged samples?
PCR: the gel images. Did the flagged samples show a band?
Library preparation and pooling: the library concentrations, and the volume of each sample that went into the pool.
Indexes: the index (barcode) of each sample, in the sample sheet you sent to the sequencing center. The center uses these indexes to sort the reads into samples. This is called demultiplexing. A wrong or swapped index can make a sample look empty.
Plate layout: do the flagged samples share a plate, a row or a column? That points to a step that was done per plate, row or column, for example with a multichannel pipette or an index plate.
The delivery report: how many reads are “undetermined”? These are reads that the center could not assign to any sample. Many undetermined reads can point to a problem with the indexes.

Who to contact: the person who did the step that looks off. That can be you, a technician or a student. For questions about indexes and undetermined reads, contact the sequencing center.









FixBlanks have many reads, or a positive control has very few (4e)






The gel images and concentrations of the controls.
The position of the controls on the plate. Was a blank next to a sample with a lot of DNA?
Keep the blanks and controls in your data, and write down which ones had reads. They are used later in the analysis to recognize contamination.

Who to contact: the person who did the lab work.









FixSome samples have clearly worse quality than the rest (Step 5)






Do the same samples also have few reads (Step 4)? Then the low quality is probably a side effect of the low read number. Follow the box for few reads instead.
Is the quality only lower towards the end of the reads? This is usually handled later, in your analysis, with a quality trimming step. Trimming cuts off the low-quality ends of the reads, and filtering removes reads that are too poor overall. Write down which samples look worse, so you can check them again after trimming.
Keep in mind that trimming has a limit. In most amplicon analyses, R1 and R2 of each read pair are joined into one sequence later. This only works if the two reads still overlap after trimming. If you have to cut off a lot, they may no longer overlap.
Is the quality low already at the start of the reads, in many samples? Or does the delivery report mention a problem with the run? Then the problem is probably in the sequencing run itself.

Who to contact: the sequencing center, if the quality is low from the start of the reads, or if the delivery report mentions a problem. For a drop towards the end of the reads, you usually do not need to contact anyone.




What to bring
Whoever you contact, these help them to understand the problem:

read_counts.tsv (copy it to your computer with scp, as in Step 5b)
multiqc_report.html, if you made one
Your sample list, with the plate layout if you have it
The delivery email from the sequencing center, with any reports that came with it
Your notes: what you ran and what you saw



If you are still stuck
Maybe the checks above do not explain the problem. Maybe you do not know who did a step, or something else surprised you. Then talk to your PI. You can also contact Nina. This is especially useful if the samples cannot be sequenced again, and you want to discuss whether the data can still be used.

title: A first look at your data
text:
Now your own data
You now run the same steps on your own data. Most commands stay the same. This section explains what changes.

Make a project folder
Give every sequencing run its own folder. Here it is called seq_qc. If you check several runs, use names like seq_qc_run2026_10.

# On Crunchomics: go to your personal folder
cd ~/personal

# Make the project folder with a data and a results folder inside
mkdir -p seq_qc/data seq_qc/results

# Move into the project folder
cd seq_qc

# Check: you should be in /home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc (with your UvAnetID), and see data and results
pwd
ls

From now on, run every command from inside the seq_qc folder. If you log out and in again, first go back with cd ~/personal/seq_qc.


Get your data onto Crunchomics
Choose the option that fits how you got your data.

Download from a linkCopy from your own computer


Many sequencing centers send a download link. You can download directly onto Crunchomics, which is faster than downloading to your laptop first:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc: go into the data folder
cd data

# Download the file. Replace the link with the one from your sequencing center. Keep the quotes.
# Note in your notes where the link came from and when you got it
# -L: if the link sends you on to another address, follow it
# -O: save the file under its own name
curl -L -O "https://link-from-your-sequencing-center"

# Check: the file is there, with a realistic size
ls -lh

# Go back to the project folder
cd ..

If the file name looks strange, for example download?token=..., rename it with mv, as in Tidy up: mv and rmdir.


If the data is already on your computer, copy it with scp, as in Step 2. Copy what you got from the sequencing center as it is: one file (for example a .tar.gz) or a whole folder. Run this in a terminal on your own computer, from the folder that contains it:

# On your computer: copy one file into the data folder on Crunchomics
# Replace your_file.tar.gz with the name of your file, and both instances of uvanetid with your UvAnetID
scp your_file.tar.gz uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc/data/

# Or: copy a whole folder. -r copies the folder with everything inside it
# Replace your_folder with the name of your folder
scp -r your_folder uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/uvanetid/personal/seq_qc/data/




If you now have one big file ending in .tar.gz in data, unpack it with tar, as in Step 2:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc: unpack the file into the data folder
# Replace your_file.tar.gz with the name of your file. -C data: unpack into the data folder
tar -xzf data/your_file.tar.gz -C data

# Check: what is in data now? The files may sit in one or more folders
ls data

If you have a file ending in .zip instead, unpack it with unzip:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc: unpack the zip file into the data folder
# Replace your_file.zip with the name of your file. -d data: unpack into the data folder
unzip data/your_file.zip -d data

# Check: what is in data now?
ls data

The .tar.gz or .zip file stays in data. That is fine: the commands on this page only use files that end in .fastq.gz. Keep the file as a backup of what you got from the sequencing center.
If you are unsure what kind of file you have, ask Nina. Then continue with Find your fastq files.


Find your fastq files
Every sequencing center organizes its data in its own way. Your fastq.gz files may sit directly in data, or one or more folders deeper. Each */ in a path stands for one folder level. See Paths: going deeper into folders if you need a reminder of how paths work. First look at what is there, then count the fastq.gz files at each level:

# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc
# Look: what is directly in data?
ls data

# Look one and two folders deeper. head shows only the first 20 lines
ls data/* | head -20
ls data/*/* | head -20

# Count the fastq.gz files at each level
# At the levels without files, you see "No such file or directory" and the count 0. That is fine
ls data/*.fastq.gz | wc -l
ls data/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l
ls data/*/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

ls data/* lists the content of each folder in data, one folder after the other, with the folder name above it. This shows you how your data is organized. The count with a number above 0 tells you at which level your fastq.gz files are.






ImportantImportant: check how your files are named





All commands on this page expect file names that end in .fastq.gz, with _R1 and _R2 in the name, for example Sample1_R1.fastq.gz. Some sequencing centers name their files differently, for example Sample1_1.fq.gz and Sample1_2.fq.gz. Then the counts above, or the counts of R1 and R2 files in Step 2, are 0, and later commands find no files. Look at the file names in the ls output. If they are named differently, contact Nina to adapt the commands.



If the files sit deeper than data, move them up with mv, as in Move the files out of the sample folders. Use the path with the right number of */, for example mv -n data/*/*/*.fastq.gz data/. Count again afterwards. The count directly in data should be the same as the count before the move. If it is lower, some files may have the same name. Ask Nina how to adapt the command.


Check your files
Run the commands from Check: are all files there? in Step 2. Your fastq.gz files should now sit directly in the data folder.
Compare the numbers with your sample list:

R1 count = number of samples you sent
R1 count = R2 count

If a sample is missing, or there are files you did not expect, note it down. Step 6 says what to check and who to contact.


Repeat Steps 3 to 6
Run Steps 3 to 6 again, inside seq_qc, with these changes:

Everywhere: you work in seq_qc instead of seq_qc_practice. In the scp commands of Step 5, replace seq_qc_practice with seq_qc in the path on Crunchomics (after the :). On your own computer, you can keep using ~/seq_qc_practice, or cd into another folder of your choice.
Step 4a and 4b: use your own seqkit table from Step 3. In the three commands that use seqkit_stats_practice.tsv, replace it with results/seqkit/seqkit_stats.tsv. For example:

# Your own data: the table from Step 3
cut -f1,4 results/seqkit/seqkit_stats.tsv | grep "_R1" | sort -t$'\t' -k2,2n > results/read_counts.tsv

Step 4c: no change. counts=results/read_counts.tsv now points to your own read counts.
Step 4d: if your sample list says where each sample was on the plate, look the flagged samples up. Are they all in the same columns or rows?
Step 4e: adjust the names in the grep command to how you named your controls.
Step 4f (optional): your file names probably do not start with the run. Use the box below to find out if your data comes from one run or more.
Step 5b: use the commands in the second box below to pick which reports to look at. In RStudio, go to personal, then seq_qc, then results, then fastqc.







TipTip: Step 4f with your own data: one run or more?





The first line of every fastq file tells you which run it comes from (see the deeper dive for what the parts mean):

# For each R1 file: the file name and the instrument, run number and flow cell
for f in data/*_R1*.fastq.gz; do
    run=$(zcat "$f" | head -1 | cut -d':' -f1-3)
    echo -e "$(basename "$f")\t${run}"
done > results/run_per_file.tsv

# How many files per run? One line means one run, and you can skip the rest of this box
cut -f2 results/run_per_file.tsv | sort | uniq -c

If you see more than one run, make a read-count file per run. Replace FLOWCELL with a flow cell ID from the output above (the last part, for example 000000000-LT57L):

# The R1 files of one run
grep "FLOWCELL" results/run_per_file.tsv | cut -f1 > results/files_run1.txt

# Keep only these files in the read-count table
grep -F -f results/files_run1.txt results/read_counts.tsv > results/read_counts_run1.tsv
wc -l results/read_counts_run1.tsv

Then do 4c to 4e with counts=results/read_counts_run1.tsv, and repeat for the other run.









TipTip: Step 5b with your own data: which reports to pick






# On Crunchomics, inside seq_qc
# The 3 samples with the fewest reads
head -3 results/read_counts.tsv

# Samples around the median: the middle lines of the sorted list (as in Step 4c)
n_samples=$(wc -l < results/read_counts.tsv)
middle=$(( (n_samples + 1) / 2 ))
sed -n "${middle}p" results/read_counts.tsv
sed -n "$(( middle + 1 ))p" results/read_counts.tsv

For example, the report of Sample1_R1.fastq.gz is Sample1_R1_fastqc.html.



Then decide, as in Step 6.

title: The commands you need
text:
This page covers only the few commands you need for this tutorial. For most of them, you do not need to understand every detail. Copy the commands, and check that your output matches what the page tells you to expect. The exception is moving around: pwd, ls, cd and paths. Take the time to understand these. You use them all the time, and they help you find your way when a command fails. If you want to learn the command line properly, for example to explore your own data in more depth, follow the CLI workshop. Each command on this page also links to the matching section of the workshop, where you find more explanation and exercises.
On this page, you work on your own computer. You download a small set of practice data and try every command on it. On the next page, A first look at your data, you copy the same practice data to Crunchomics and do the full check. After that, you repeat the check with your own data.

title: The commands you need
text:
The practice data
The practice data comes from an ITS (a DNA region used to identify fungi) amplicon sequencing project from different soil samples. It comes from two real sequencing runs, Run1 and Run2, and it has a real problem that you explore on the next page. The sample IDs are randomized, and every file was reduced to 2% of its reads to keep it small.
You will work with 32 samples that were sequenced with Illumina, a widely used type of sequencing machine. The data is paired-end: the sequencer reads each DNA fragment from both ends. So every sample has two files:

..._R1.fastq.gz: the reads from one end of the fragments (the forward reads).
..._R2.fastq.gz: the reads from the other end (the reverse reads).

In total, that makes 64 files. A .fastq file is a text file that holds every read, with a quality score for each base. The .gz at the end means that the file is compressed to save space.
The practice data also contains seqkit_stats_practice.tsv. This is a table with the number of reads per file, for all samples of the original two runs. You look at it further down this page.

title: The commands you need
text:
Setting up a terminal
For this tutorial you need set up a terminal: a window in which you type commands (instructions to the computer) as text, instead of clicking on buttons and menus. If you have never opened a terminal, first follow Before you start of the CLI workshop:

On Windows, use a local terminal in MobaXterm.
On a Mac, use the Terminal app, which you find in Applications, in the Utilities folder. The Mac terminal uses a slightly different shell (zsh), the program that reads your commands. So a few error messages may look a bit different from the ones on this page.

If something goes wrong, see Getting unstuck at the bottom of this page.

title: The commands you need
text:
The terminal and the prompt
The terminal passes what you type to a shell, the program that reads your commands and tells the computer what to do. When the computer is ready for the next command, it shows the prompt, a line that usually ends with $.
A few things that make life easier:

Copy and paste. In many terminals, Ctrl+C does not copy, because Ctrl+C stops a command (see below). Use the right mouse button instead, or Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V. This differs between terminals, so try it once.
Tab completion. Type the first letters of a file or folder name and press Tab. The terminal completes the name for you. This saves typing and avoids typos.
Arrow up. Press the up arrow to get your previous commands back.
Comments. Everything after a # is a comment. The computer ignores it. In this tutorial, every command comes with a comment that says what it does. You can paste the comments along with the commands.

Now you are ready to type your first command.

title: The commands you need
text:
pwd: where am I?

# On your computer: print the folder you are in right now
pwd

When you open a new terminal, you start in your home folder. The path that pwd prints differs between computers. A path is the address of a folder, with folder names separated by /, something like /home/mobaxterm or /Users/yourname. The CLI workshop explains where your home folder is.

title: The commands you need
section: ls: what is in this folder?
text:
ls: what is in this folder?

# On your computer: list the files and folders in the current folder
ls

# The same, with more details: size, date, owner
# The options change how ls behaves:
# -l long list with details, -h sizes in K/M/G
ls -lh

More: ls in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
The parts of a command
Most commands on this page have up to three parts. Take ls -lh data as an example, a command like the ones you use later on this page:

The command name is the program you want to run: ls.
An option (or flag) changes how the command behaves: -lh. Options usually start with a -. Several one-letter options can be written together, so -lh is the same as -l -h.
An argument is what the command works on, often a file or a folder: data. Some commands work without an argument. For example, ls without an argument lists the folder you are in now.

Spaces separate the parts. So always put a space between the command name, the options and the arguments.
When you see a new command on this page, try to find its three parts. The comment above the command tells you what the command does.
More: the structure of a command in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
mkdir: make a folder






ImportantMobaXterm users: did you choose a permanent folder?





MobaXterm can use a temporary home folder. Then it deletes your files when you close it. Before you continue, check this with the steps in Windows + MobaXterm: choose a permanent folder on the “Before you start” page of the CLI workshop.




# On your computer, in your home folder: make a folder for the practice data, name it seq_qc_practice
mkdir seq_qc_practice

# Check if the new folder exists: 
# you should see seq_qc_practice in the list
ls -l

More: mkdir in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
cd: move into a folder

# Move into the seq_qc_practice folder
cd seq_qc_practice

# Check: the path should now end in seq_qc_practice
pwd

A few more ways to use cd. Try them, and then go back into seq_qc_practice:

# Move one folder up
cd ..

# Check where you are now 
pwd

# Move back to your home folder, from anywhere
cd

# Check where you are now 
pwd

# Go back into the practice folder: ~ is short for your home folder
cd ~/seq_qc_practice
pwd

In the beginning it is a good habit to check where you are with pwd after every cd. Most errors in this tutorial come from running a command in the wrong folder.
More: cd in the workshop

title: The commands you need
section: Get the practice data: curl and tar
text:
Get the practice data: curl and tar
The practice data can be downloaded in one single file, practice_data.tar.gz. A .tar.gz file packs many files into one and compresses them, similar to a .zip file.

# Inside seq_qc_practice: download the practice data
# -L: if the link sends you on to another address, follow it
# -O: save the file under its own name, practice_data.tar.gz
curl -L -O "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/sequencing_qc/main/data/practice_data.tar.gz"

# Check: you should see practice_data.tar.gz, with a size of about 11M (11 megabytes)
ls -lh

# Unpack the compressed folder. Used options: 
# -x extract, -z it is compressed (.gz), -f the file name follows
tar -xzf practice_data.tar.gz

# Check what changed
# you should see data, practice_data.tar.gz and seqkit_stats_practice.tsv
ls

# Check the inside of the newly generated data folder 
# you should see one folder per sample, with names like Run1_S137 
# (you learn how to count the number of files later)
ls data 

# Look inside one sample folder: you should see the R1 and R2 file of that sample
ls data/Run1_S137

The data folder contains several folders, one per sample. Each sample folder holds the sequencing files of that sample. Many sequencing centers deliver data like this. One good first sanity check is to count the number of folders or files you have per sample. You learn how to do this further down.
Keep practice_data.tar.gz. You copy it to Crunchomics on the next page. Also for your own data it is a good practice to keep a copy of your data in a safe location as a backup.

title: The commands you need
text:
Paths: going deeper into folders
In the last command, data/Run1_S137 means: the folder Run1_S137 inside the folder data. Each / takes you one folder deeper. A path that does not start with / or ~ begins in the folder you are in now. So ls data/Run1_S137 only works when you are inside seq_qc_practice.
Sequencing centers often deliver data in several layers of folders. To get a feeling for these layers, move into one sample folder and back out again:

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Move two folders deeper, into the folder of one sample
cd data/Run1_S137

# Check: the path should now end in seq_qc_practice/data/Run1_S137
pwd

# Check: you should see Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz and Run1_S137_R2.fastq.gz
ls

# Move two folders up again: each .. is one folder up
cd ../..

# Check: the path should end in seq_qc_practice again
pwd

You do not need to cd into a folder to look at it. From seq_qc_practice, ls data/Run1_S137 shows the same files. In this tutorial, you stay in one folder and write the path to the files instead.
Tab completion helps with long paths. Type ls data/ and press Tab twice. The terminal shows what is inside data. Type the first letters of a folder name, for example Run1_S13, and press Tab again to complete it. On a Mac, one Tab can be enough to show the list. If several names match, Tab completes as far as it can. Press Tab twice to see the options, then type one more letter.






TipTip: folder names with spaces (optional)





Some folders from a sequencing center have a space in the name, for example Project 1234. The terminal reads a space as the end of a name, because spaces separate the parts of a command. So ls data/Project 1234 looks for two things, data/Project and 1234, and you get No such file or directory.
Put the path in quotes, or use Tab completion. Tab completion adds a \ before the space, which also works:

# Both commands list the folder "Project 1234" inside data
ls "data/Project 1234"
ls data/Project\ 1234

# With a wildcard, keep the * outside the quotes
ls "data/Project 1234"/*.fastq.gz

There is no folder with a space in the practice data, so you cannot try this here.

title: The commands you need
text:
Wildcards: *
A * in a file name means “any text”. It is called a wildcard. This way of writing file names lets you select many files at once.

# Look for R1 files directly in data: data/*_R1.fastq.gz matches every file in data that ends in _R1.fastq.gz
# You get "No such file or directory": 
# that is because the files are not in the data folder but one level deeper, in the sample folders
ls data/*_R1.fastq.gz

# Look one level deeper: the first * stands for any folder name in data
ls data/*/*_R1.fastq.gz

The last command lists all files in the folder, from data/Run1_S137/Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz to data/Run2_ITS100/Run2_ITS100_R1.fastq.gz.
More: wildcards in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
Counting: wc -l and the pipe |
The next commands help you check quickly how many files a folder holds.
wc -l counts lines. The pipe | sends the output of one command into the next command. Together, they let you count things, for example the number of files:

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Count the fastq.gz files in the sample folders: 
# when ls sends its output into a pipe, it prints one name per line, and wc -l counts the lines
# Expected: 64
ls data/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

# Count only the R1 files. Expected: 32
ls data/*/*_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l

You will use this a lot. After each step, you count what you have and compare it with what you expect. For now, the command tells you that you work with 64 files from 32 samples. That is what you expect, so you can continue.
If you ever see fewer samples than what you expect then this often means an incomplete download. To check this, download the file again and repeat the steps from above to see whether this recovers your files.
More: wc and pipes in the workshop

title: The commands you need
section: Looking at files: head and less
text:
Looking at files: head and less
seqkit_stats_practice.tsv is a table with the number of reads in every file of the original sequencing runs. A .tsv file is a table where tabs separate the columns. You make a table like this yourself on the next page. For now, you learn how to look inside a file.

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Show the first 10 lines of the table
head seqkit_stats_practice.tsv

# Count the lines. Expected: 729 (one header line and 728 files)
wc -l seqkit_stats_practice.tsv

# Scroll through the whole table. Use the arrow keys, and press q to quit
# -S keeps long lines on one line, so tables stay readable
less -S seqkit_stats_practice.tsv

In this file you work with 728 files, not 64. That is because the table covers all 364 samples of the original runs, and the practice data is 32 of them.
The first line of seqkit_stats_practice.tsv is the header, with the column names. The fourth column, num_seqs, is the number of reads in each file.
More: head and less in the workshop

title: The commands you need
section: Searching and selecting: grep and cut
text:
Searching and selecting: grep and cut
Sometimes you want to search a file for a word, for example to count how many samples each run has. grep does this: it keeps only the lines that contain a word or a piece of text.
Another useful command is cut, which keeps only some columns of a table. This command can be useful to extract only the relevant columns of a larger table.
Try both on seqkit_stats_practice.tsv:

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Show only the lines for sample Run1_S137. Expected: 2 lines, one for R1 and one for R2
grep "Run1_S137" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv

# Count the lines of run 2. Expected: 248 (124 samples, with an R1 and an R2 file each)
grep "Run2_" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | wc -l

# Keep only column 1 (the file name) and column 4 (the number of reads)
# -f: the columns to keep, separated by a comma
cut -f1,4 seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | head

These commands become very handy once you combine them with a pipe to answer a question about your data. For example: how many reads do the blanks have?

# The lines with Blank in the name, and only the file name and number of reads
# Expected: 8 lines (4 blanks, R1 and R2), with between 41 and 4561 reads
grep "Blank" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | cut -f1,4

Good to know: grep is case-sensitive: If you had used grep "blank", you would have found nothing, because the file names use Blank. With grep -i, upper and lower case count as the same. You use this on the next page.
More: grep and cut in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
Saving output to a file: >
So far, every command printed its result to the screen. With >, you save the result in a file instead. On the next page, you use this to save your read counts.






ImportantImportant: > overwrites without asking





If the file after > already exists, > replaces its content without a warning. Check the file name before you press Enter.




# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Save the file names and read numbers of the blanks in a new file, blanks.tsv
# Nothing is printed to the screen: the output goes into the file
grep "Blank" seqkit_stats_practice.tsv | cut -f1,4 > blanks.tsv

# Check: blanks.tsv is there
ls

# Check: 8 lines, the same as on the screen before
wc -l blanks.tsv
head blanks.tsv

More: redirection in the workshop

title: The commands you need
text:
Tidy up: mv and rmdir
mv moves files. Here, you move all fastq.gz files out of the sample folders, directly into data. The mv command is handy whenever you want to re-organize data for a cleaner folder structure.






ImportantImportant: mv also renames





If the last name in an mv command is not an existing folder, mv renames your file to that name. For example, with a typo, mv sample_R1.fastq.gz dta renames the file to dta. To prevent this, end a folder name with /, as in data/. Then mv stops with an error if the folder does not exist.




# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Move all fastq.gz files from the sample folders up into the data folder
# -n: never overwrite a file that already exists in data
mv -n data/*/*.fastq.gz data/

# Check: count the fastq.gz files directly in data. Expected: 64
ls data/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

# Check: count the fastq.gz files left in the sample folders. Expected: 0
# You also see "ls: cannot access ... No such file or directory". That is fine: there are no files left to list
ls data/*/*.fastq.gz | wc -l

More: mv in the workshop
The sample folders are now empty. rmdir removes empty folders. It never removes a folder that still contains files, so it is a safe way to clean up:

# On your computer, inside seq_qc_practice
# Remove the empty sample folders: data/*/ matches every folder in data
rmdir data/*/

# Check: look at the first names, and count everything in data
# Expected: only fastq.gz files, 64 in total
ls data | head
ls data | wc -l

If a sample folder still contains a file, rmdir says Directory not empty and keeps that folder. Look inside with ls to see what is left.

title: The commands you need
text:
Getting unstuck

A command does not finish, or the prompt does not come back: press Ctrl+C to stop it.
The prompt changes to > (or dquote> on a Mac) and nothing happens: the terminal waits for the rest of a command. This often happens when a quote " is missing, for example when you copied only part of a line. Press Ctrl+C, then copy and paste the whole command again.
command not found: the computer does not know this command. Check the spelling. On your own computer, it can also mean that the tool is not installed.
Nothing is printed: for many commands, such as mkdir, cd and mv, no output means that the command worked. Use ls or pwd to check the result.
An error message: read it. It usually says what went wrong, for example No such file or directory means the file name is wrong, or you are in the wrong folder (check with pwd and ls).

More: error messages and Ctrl+C in the workshop
Using an AI chat tool? You do not need one for this tutorial. Every command is tested, and the boxes tell you what to expect. If you are stuck, use the tips above, or ask Nina. If you still want to ask an AI chat tool, for example to explain an error message, read Using LLMs to understand and check code in the CLI workshop first. At the UvA, use UvA AI Chat, and never paste your sequencing data into it.

title: Welcome
text:
This short tutorial is designed to help you take a first look at your sequencing data, shortly after receiving it, and decide one thing: does anything look off?
To follow this tutorial you do not need to know the command line. You copy and paste a small number of commands, and you look at a few numbers and one report. You first work through all steps with practice data from a real sequencing run with a real problem, and then repeat them with your own data.

title: Welcome
section: Why look at your data right away?
text:
Why look at your data right away?
Assume you send some data of for sequencing. It often takes some weeks to get the sequencing data back and you have other projects to work on. Often this means that the data won’t get inspected months after receiving it. However, after you finally find some time to start your analysis you realize something is wrong, and that many of your samples have very few reads and you have to figure out what is going on.
This can become a problem: If you wait for a long time to inspect the quality of your sequencing data it can become much harder to figure out what went wrong, or how to fix it. Maybe the PCR products are no longer available, maybe you realize your lab notes are incomplete or that the person at the sequencing center who handled the data is gone.
If you look at the read numbers in the first week, the problem would have been visible much faster, while it still might be easier to fix a potential issue.

title: Welcome
text:
What you will do

Learn some basic commands to interact with your computer
Copy data to Crunchomics, the UvA computer cluster
Count the reads in every sample, and check for samples with far fewer reads than the rest
Make quality reports with FastQC, and look at a few of them in your browser
Decide whether everything looks fine, or whether something needs a closer look. For the second case, the tutorial gives a checklist and says who to contact

You do these steps twice. First with practice data from a real sequencing run with a real problem. For every step, the tutorial tells you what you should see. Then you can repeat the same steps with your own data.

title: Deeper dive (optional)
section: What a fastq file looks like
text:
What a fastq file looks like
A fastq.gz file is compressed, so head on it shows unreadable characters. zcat unpacks the file and prints the text to the screen, without changing the file itself. Send its output into head to see only the start.
On a Mac, use gzcat instead of zcat, here and in the rest of this page.

# Show the first 4 lines of one fastq file: this is the first read
zcat data/Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz | head -4

Every read takes up 4 lines:

The read name, or header. It starts with @ and holds information about the sequencing machine and the run. The next section explains its parts.
The sequence: the bases A, C, G and T.
A +.
The quality: one character per base. Each character stands for how sure the machine is about that base.

Because every read has 4 lines, you can count the reads in a file. Count the lines and divide by 4:

# Count the lines in one fastq file. Expected: 9940, so 9940 / 4 = 2485 reads
zcat data/Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l

On the main page, seqkit does this count for all files at once.
More: zcat and fastq files in the CLI workshop

title: Deeper dive (optional)
section: What the read header tells you
text:
What the read header tells you
Every read in a fastq file starts with a header line that begins with @. For Illumina data, the header holds information about where and how the read was sequenced.

# The first header line of one practice file
zcat data/Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz | head -1

It looks something like this:
@M08325:104:000000000-LT57L:1:1101:15589:1335 1:N:0:GTGTATGCGT
The parts before the space are separated by ::








Part
Example
Meaning




Instrument
M08325
The sequencer. An ID starting with M is a MiSeq


Run number
104
The how-manyth run on this instrument


Flow cell
000000000-LT57L
The flow cell (the glass slide the DNA was sequenced on)


Lane
1
The lane on the flow cell


Tile, x, y
1101:15589:1335
Where on the flow cell this read was



The parts after the space:








Part
Example
Meaning




Read
1
1 for the R1 file, 2 for the R2 file


Filtered
N
N: the read passed the quality filter


Control
0
0 for normal reads


Index
GTGTATGCGT
The barcode as it was read by the sequencer



Exercise: Look at the first header of a Run1_ and a Run2_ file. Were they sequenced on the same instrument? In the same run?
Exercise: The index at the end is the barcode that was used to sort the read into its sample. Count the indices in the first 1000 reads of a good sample and of a failed sample:

# Count the barcodes in the first 1000 reads (4000 lines) of one file, most common first
# A good sample: how many reads carry the most common barcode?
zcat data/Run1_S137_R1.fastq.gz | head -4000 | awk 'NR % 4 == 1' | cut -d':' -f10 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# A failed sample: compare with the good sample
zcat data/Run1_S158_R1.fastq.gz | head -4000 | awk 'NR % 4 == 1' | cut -d':' -f10 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

What do you notice?






AnswerPractice data: compare with your result





Good sample, Run1_S137:
    919 ACGTATCATC
     18 CCGTATCATC
     10 TCGTATCATC
      8 ACGTAGCATC
      5 ACGTATCACC
      4 GCGTATCATC
      4 ACGTATCATT
      4 ACGTATCATA
      4 ACGTAACATC
      3 ACTTATCATC
Failed sample, Run1_S158:
      4 TGATGTATGT
      2 TGGTGTATGT
      1 TTATGTATGT
      1 TGTTGTATGT
      1 TGATGTAAGT
      1 GGATGTATGT
Good sample: 919 of the 1000 reads carry the same barcode, ACGTATCATC. The other barcodes differ from it in one letter. In these reads, the sequencer misread one base of the barcode. The software that sorts the reads into samples allows for small reading errors like this, so these reads still end up in the right sample.
Failed sample: the file has only 10 reads, so the command shows all of them. Only 4 of the 10 reads carry the most common barcode, TGATGTATGT. The other 6 each differ from it in one letter.
So in the good sample, more than 9 in 10 reads carry the exact barcode. In the failed sample, fewer than half do. When a sample has almost no reads of its own, the reads with a misread barcode make up a much larger part of the few reads it has.
To check which barcode belongs to which sample, look at the sample sheet from the sequencing center.

title: Deeper dive (optional)
section: A good and a failed sample in FastQC
text:
A good and a failed sample in FastQC
This section compares the FastQC report of a good sample, S2, with a failed sample, S91.
The plots below come from the full sequencing data, not from the practice data. The practice data has far fewer reads per sample. With fewer reads, each point in a plot is based on less data, so your FastQC plots of the practice data look noisier: the lines are more jagged and the boxes jump around more. Look at the overall pattern, not at single points. Your own data will likely have more reads and look closer to the plots on this page.
FastQC gives every panel a green tick, an orange exclamation mark or a red cross. Its limits were made for random pieces of DNA, for example from whole genome sequencing. Amplicon reads are not random: they are copies of one short DNA region. So with amplicon data, a good sample also gets several red crosses. Here, the good and the failed sample both get a red cross on 7 of the 11 panels. Don’t count red crosses. Instead, compare a good and a suspicious sample side by side, as below.

Per base sequence quality



Good sample: S2





Failed sample: S91


This plot shows the quality along the read, from the first base (left) to the last base (right). The quality score (y-axis) says how sure the sequencer is about a base. A score of 30 means 1 wrong base in 1,000. A score of 20 means 1 wrong base in 100. The background shows how FastQC rates the scores: green is very good, orange is reasonable, red is poor.
At each position:

The yellow box holds the middle half of the reads.
The red line in the box is the median.
The whiskers (thin lines) show where the lowest 10% and the highest 10% of the reads start.
The blue line connects the mean scores.

Good sample: the boxes stay at the top up to about base 200. After that, the quality falls, and the last bases end in the red zone. This is normal for long reads, because the sequencing chemistry wears out as the read gets longer. Later analysis steps cut off these low-quality ends. FastQC still gives a red cross.
Failed sample: the quality falls much earlier. At about base 70, the mean drops, and the lower whiskers already reach the red zone. The boxes are also wider along the whole read. So the reads in this sample have lower quality overall, not only at the end.
What to look at: where the quality starts to fall, not the color at the end of the read.


Per sequence quality scores



Good sample: S2





Failed sample: S91


This plot gives each read one number: its mean quality over all its bases. The x-axis shows the mean quality, and the y-axis shows how many reads have it.
Good sample: one tall peak at a quality of about 36. There is a small bump at 21 to 23: a few reads with low quality. Every run has some of these, so this is normal.
Failed sample: two peaks. One is at 34, and a second one is at 21 to 22. About a quarter of the reads have a low quality.
FastQC gives both samples a green tick, because it only checks where the highest peak is. Still, this plot shows the difference between the samples most clearly.
What to look at: one peak at high quality is good. A second peak at low quality means that a large part of the reads is poor.


Per base sequence content



Good sample: S2





Failed sample: S91


This plot shows, for each position in the read, how many percent of the reads have an A, C, G or T. In random DNA, the four lines would run flat and close together. Amplicon reads are different. They all start with the same primer, and they come from a small number of organisms.
Good sample: in the first 9 positions, one base reaches almost 100% at each position. Read the peaks from left to right: C, T, T, G, G, T, C, A, T. This is the start of the ITS1F primer, CTTGGTCATTTAGAGGAAGTAA. After the primer, the lines go up and down, because most reads come from a few organisms. FastQC gives a red cross, but for amplicon data this is expected.
Failed sample: the primer is not clearly visible. At position 1, about 57% of the reads have a G and about 34% have a C. The C fits the ITS1F primer (CTT...). The G fits the 16S primer 515F (GTG...). So this ITS sample also holds 16S reads, probably from other samples on the same run.
What to look at: in amplicon data, the first bases of the reads should spell out your primer. If they don’t, the sample holds reads that don’t belong there.
More: FastQC help, one page per panel
